title: If instance App1 updates a value, how does instance App2 see the change (there is no shared JVM memory) — via a shared database as the source of truth, a distributed cache like Redis, or a Kafka event that other instances consume to update local state/invalidate caches?
shortTitle: How one instance sees a change another instance made

s1_definition.profdef: When a service runs as multiple instances, each instance is a separate JVM with its own heap, so a value updated in one instance's memory is invisible to another; in-process state and local caches do not propagate across instances. To make App2 observe App1's update you externalize the state through one of three mechanisms: a shared database that is the single source of truth every instance reads, a distributed cache like Redis that all instances share, or a Kafka event that App1 publishes and other instances consume to update their local state or invalidate their local caches — most production systems combine the database as source of truth with Redis and events for freshness.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has two identical counters, each with its own private notepad. If the clerk at counter one writes "Rajesh's new balance is 950000" on their own notepad, the clerk at counter two has no idea — their notepad still says 1000000. For counter two to know, they must either both read from the central ledger in the vault (shared database), both check a shared whiteboard on the wall that everyone updates (Redis), or counter one must shout an announcement "Rajesh's balance changed" that counter two hears and acts on (Kafka event). Private notepads never sync by themselves.
s1_definition.oneliner: Separate instances share no memory, so a change becomes visible only by externalizing it — through a shared database, a distributed cache, or an event that other instances consume.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a service runs as multiple instances, each instance is a separate JVM with its own heap, so a value updated in one instance's memory is invisible to another; in-process state and local caches do not propagate across instances. To make App2 observe App1's update you externalize the state through one of three mechanisms: a shared database that is the single source of truth every instance reads, a distributed cache like Redis that all instances share, or a Kafka event that App1 publishes and other instances consume to update their local state or invalidate their local caches — most production systems combine the database as source of truth with Redis and events for freshness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has two identical counters, each with its own private notepad. If the clerk at counter one writes "Rajesh's new balance is 950000" on their own notepad, the clerk at counter two has no idea — their notepad still says 1000000. For counter two to know, they must either both read from the central ledger in the vault (shared database), both check a shared whiteboard on the wall that everyone updates (Redis), or counter one must shout an announcement "Rajesh's balance changed" that counter two hears and acts on (Kafka event). Private notepads never sync by themselves.

**One line to remember:** Separate instances share no memory, so a change becomes visible only by externalizing it — through a shared database, a distributed cache, or an event that other instances consume.

sections.s2_technical:
The fundamental fact is process isolation. Each instance of a service is a distinct operating-system process running its own JVM with its own heap. A field updated in App1, a value stored in a static map, a Spring singleton's in-memory state, or an in-process cache like a plain Caffeine or ConcurrentHashMap, all live only in App1's heap. App2 has its own separate copy and never sees App1's change. This is why keeping mutable shared state in instance memory is a classic bug when you scale from one instance to many: it works in development with a single instance and silently breaks in production behind a load balancer, because different requests hit different instances with different local state.

The first and most important mechanism is a shared database as the source of truth. Instead of trusting instance memory, every instance writes the authoritative value to a shared database and reads it back when needed. App1 commits Rajesh's new balance to the database; App2, on its next request, reads the balance from the database and sees the new value. This is the correct default for anything that must be consistent and durable, like money, because the database is the one authoritative copy and gives you transactions and strong consistency within it. The cost is a database round trip on every read, which can be a bottleneck for hot, frequently-read values.

The second mechanism is a distributed cache like Redis. Redis is an external, shared, in-memory store that all instances talk to over the network, so a value written by App1 is immediately readable by App2. It is used both as a fast read cache in front of the database (cache-aside) and as a place to hold genuinely shared transient state like sessions, rate-limit counters, and distributed locks. Because it is shared and fast, it solves cross-instance visibility for hot data without hammering the database. The subtlety is invalidation: when the underlying value changes, the cache must be updated or evicted so instances do not serve stale data, which is where TTLs and event-driven invalidation come in.

The third mechanism is a Kafka event. When App1 makes a change, it publishes an event, and all other instances — as members of a consumer group or via a broadcast pattern — consume it and react by updating their own local state or invalidating their local caches. This is push rather than pull: instead of App2 repeatedly asking the database "has this changed," App1 tells everyone when it does. Events are ideal for propagating changes that drive local read models, for cache invalidation across instances, and for triggering downstream work. The trade-off is eventual consistency, because there is a small delay between App1's publish and App2's consume, so this is right for data that tolerates brief staleness, not for the authoritative balance read inside a transfer.

In practice you combine them, and a senior engineer explains the layering. The shared database is the source of truth for correctness and durability. Redis sits in front for low-latency reads of hot data, populated cache-aside and bounded by a TTL. Kafka events propagate changes so other instances invalidate or refresh their caches and local read models promptly rather than waiting for a TTL to expire. The guiding rule is never rely on instance-local memory for state that must be shared, decide per value whether strong consistency (read the database) or eventual consistency (cache plus events) is acceptable, and keep money on the strongly-consistent path.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India runs the balance service as two instances, App1 and App2, behind a load balancer. Rajesh's transfer is processed by App1, and a subsequent balance check is routed to App2.

Problem 1 — App1 updates Rajesh's balance only in its local in-memory cache. App2, handling the next read, has its own stale local cache and returns the old balance. This is the process-isolation bug: local memory does not propagate.

Problem 2 — The fix layer one is the shared database as source of truth. App1 commits the new balance to the database. App2 reads from the database and sees the correct value. Correct but a database hit on every read.

Problem 3 — The fix layer two adds Redis and a Kafka event. App1 writes the database, publishes a BalanceChanged event, and the event causes every instance to invalidate its local cache. App2 then serves the fresh value from Redis quickly, and only falls back to the database on a cache miss. This gives both speed and cross-instance freshness.

What the code will do: a runnable demo creates two instances sharing a `SharedDatabase` and a `RedisCache`, each with its own `LocalCache`. It first shows the broken case where App1 updates only its local cache and App2 reads stale. Then it shows App1 committing to the shared database and publishing a `BalanceChangedEvent` on an `EventBus` that both instances consume to invalidate their local caches, after which App2 reads the fresh value.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two instances App1 and App2, both serving Rajesh's balance, starting at Rs.1,000,000.

Step 1: Both instances read the balance and populate their own local caches from the shared store, so each local cache holds Rs.1,000,000.

Step 2 (broken): App1 updates only its own local cache to Rs.950,000. This change lives purely in App1's heap. App2's local cache is untouched.

Step 3 (broken): App2 serves a balance read from its own local cache and returns the stale Rs.1,000,000. This is the process-isolation failure — local memory never propagates.

Step 4 (correct): App1 performs a proper update to Rs.900,000. It writes the shared database (the source of truth), refreshes the shared Redis cache, updates its own local cache, and publishes a BalanceChanged event.

Step 5 (correct): App2 consumes the BalanceChanged event and evicts its stale local cache entry for Rajesh. Its local copy is now gone, so the next read will not serve stale data.

Step 6 (correct): App2 reads the balance. Its local cache is empty, so it reads from the shared Redis cache (or the database on a miss) and returns the fresh Rs.900,000. App2 now sees App1's change because the change was externalized and propagated.

Final output:

```
16:00:00 INFO    [App1] loaded SAV2001 = Rs.1000000 (from shared store)
16:00:00 INFO    [App2] loaded SAV2001 = Rs.1000000 (from shared store)
16:00:00 INFO    ===== BROKEN: App1 updates LOCAL memory only =====
16:00:00 WARNING [App1] updated LOCAL cache only SAV2001 = Rs.950000 (others won't see it)
16:00:00 INFO    [App2] local hit SAV2001 = Rs.1000000
16:00:00 INFO    ===== CORRECT: DB source of truth + event-driven invalidation =====
16:00:00 INFO    [App1] committed DB + Redis + published BalanceChanged SAV2001 = Rs.900000
16:00:00 INFO    [App2] consumed BalanceChanged → evicted local cache for SAV2001
16:00:00 INFO    [App2] loaded SAV2001 = Rs.900000 (from shared store)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── BROKEN: local memory only ──
  App1 heap: SAV2001 = 950,000   (updateLocalOnly)
  App2 heap: SAV2001 = 1,000,000 (never told)  →  read returns STALE

  ── CORRECT: externalize + propagate ──
  App1.updateBalance(SAV2001, 900,000)
    │ 1) write Shared DB (source of truth)   900,000
    │ 2) refresh Redis                        900,000
    │ 3) publish BalanceChanged event
    ▼
  EventBus / Kafka (broadcast)
    │
    ▼
  App2.onBalanceChanged() → evict local cache(SAV2001)
    │
    ▼
  App2.readBalance(SAV2001)
    local miss → Redis 900,000 (or DB on miss) → FRESH
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The starting point is process isolation: when a service runs as multiple instances, each instance is a separate JVM with its own heap, so a value updated in one instance's memory is simply invisible to the others. A field, a static map, a Spring singleton's state, or an in-process cache like Caffeine all live only in that one instance's heap, and another instance has its own separate copy. This is why keeping mutable shared state in instance memory is a classic scaling bug — it works with a single instance in development and silently breaks in production behind a load balancer, because consecutive requests land on different instances with different local state.

To make App2 observe App1's change, I externalize the state, and there are three mechanisms. The first and most important is a shared database as the source of truth: every instance writes the authoritative value to the database and reads it back, so App1 commits Rajesh's new balance and App2 reads it and sees the new value. This is the correct default for anything that must be consistent and durable, like money, because the database is the one authoritative copy with transactions and strong consistency; the cost is a database round trip on every read. The second is a distributed cache like Redis, an external shared in-memory store all instances talk to, so a value App1 writes is immediately readable by App2, used both as a fast cache in front of the database and for genuinely shared transient state like sessions, rate-limit counters, and locks. The third is a Kafka event: when App1 changes something it publishes an event and every other instance consumes it and reacts by updating its local state or invalidating its local cache, which is push instead of pull, so App2 learns promptly instead of polling.

In practice I layer all three. The shared database is the source of truth for correctness and durability, Redis sits in front for low-latency reads of hot data with a TTL, and Kafka events propagate changes so other instances invalidate or refresh their caches quickly rather than waiting for a TTL. The decision per value is whether strong consistency is required, in which case I read the database, or whether eventual consistency is acceptable, in which case the cache plus events are enough, and I always keep money on the strongly-consistent path.

I hit this directly at National Bank of India when we scaled the balance service to multiple instances. Initially an instance updated Rajesh's balance only in its local cache, and a follow-up read routed to another instance returned the stale balance, which is exactly the process-isolation bug. We fixed it by making every update write the shared database as the source of truth, refresh Redis, and publish a BalanceChanged event that all instances consume to evict their local caches, so the next read on any instance either hit the fresh Redis value or fell back to the database, and never served a stale local copy again.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: separate instances share no memory, so a change in one is invisible to another unless I externalize it — through a shared database as the source of truth for consistent durable data, a distributed cache like Redis for fast shared reads, and Kafka events to propagate changes and invalidate other instances' caches — and I never rely on instance-local memory for state that must be shared.
